name: Bianca Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bianca, thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the coastal crew out of Port Ellery, so salt air eats everything we put up. A normal day is replacing corroded clamps and insulators on the sea-front lines, or a pole the council truck backed into. When the autumn gales come we're out for days putting the town back together. I like that it's real work you can see, and I hate the paperwork on the tablet at the end of the day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Daniel last year. He works at his dad's boatyard, fixing hulls and engines. We rent a flat above the chip shop while we save for a house, but honestly we've got under a month put by, because we paid for the wedding ourselves. I use AI now and then, mostly to tidy up the church newsletter I help with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no surprise, most new things get oversold. I'd say it at work and at church coffee, and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much. The worry is still money: we want kids in two years and we can't save fast enough on my wage, and the boatyard has quiet winters. The flat's damp and the landlord won't fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, take all the gale call-outs, and try to save two hundred a month for a house deposit. I'd ask the foreman about the next pay grade, because I've been on the same one three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but stretched. It's the normal worry of being young and broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a quiet winter at the boatyard mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Daniel's hours at his dad's boatyard drop by a third from November to February, so the gales are almost a blessing. My overtime carries us through those months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you moved up a grade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody's left the crew in three years. You wait for dead men's shoes, as the old boys say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, and you get on with it. If the company brings in better tools, fine, as long as they don't forget who climbs the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my climbing is safe for years, but the office gets thinner. Fewer planners means slower repairs and longer waits for parts. And the boatyard might lose business if AI starts selling boats and booking repairs online, but probably not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app the company uses, once the others have sorted out the bugs. I'd keep saving for the house. And I'd encourage Daniel to get his marine engine certificate so the boatyard can take bigger jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. My job feels safe, but things around it are moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the tablet paperwork, yes, if it saved me twenty minutes a day. No point being the guinea pig with new apps. I'd wait to see the lads use it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jan in stores, who orders all our parts. If a computer does the ordering, Jan's out, and Jan's got three kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and companies should take care of their people. Not the government handing out money, but firms training their own staff. I'd say that at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I have till 2031 before robots climb, and I'd be 32 with maybe a baby. The office goes in 2028. The boatyard might be safer for longer because every hull is different, but who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put off having kids, which would break my heart. I'd save every penny and ask Daniel's dad if I could learn the boatyard work, in case the line job goes. And I'd still take every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like watching the barometer drop before a gale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Daniel about putting off kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Daniel straight, after Sunday lunch at his parents'. He'd be sad but he'd understand. We'd pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for retraining if nothing else. I'd rather family helps family.

The **boatyard** might be safer for longer, but nobody knows.
do: **Put off** having children for a few years.

fieldNote: She'd **delay children**, which she calls her most painful choice.

She prefers **firms and family** over state help.

steps.text: Put off having children until the job picture is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's be sensible and plan. I'd tell the younger ones to learn a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2034 for robots feels manageable. I'd be 35, maybe with one child. I'd have time to save and learn something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, save for the house, and start learning boatyard work on Saturdays. Maybe in a few years get a welding ticket, since it's useful in both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but hopeful. It feels like we could get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try for kids in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three. Family's the point of all this, so we'd wait three years for kids, not much later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan fall apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the boatyard struggled at the same time. Then both incomes would be in trouble.

fieldNote: She'd delay children only **a year**, not more, with five years' warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and we should be grateful for the warning. I'd encourage people to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I can live with. Robots come about 2039, I'd be 40, probably with kids at school. I'd have time to build up skills and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, save steadily, and learn boatyard work gradually. Maybe use AI a bit more for the paperwork once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough, a bit uneasy. Money's still tight now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd have kids in two years like we planned. Ten years is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill people need, work hard, and don't rely on anyone else. Same as my parents told me.

fieldNote: She keeps her **kids plan** on track with a decade's warning.
Her advice to future children reflects her **traditional values**.
**Thin savings** and a damp rented flat keep her from full calm.

steps.text: Have children in two years as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would mess up our plans for kids. What would help is companies training their own workers and some help with housing for young families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small towns. My town, Port Ellery, depends on a few jobs. If those jobs go, the town empties.

**Children** are her central plan, and the fast picture would push them back.
She's **uneasy** in calm pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028 and 2031.
